title: Bandwidth steering and backpressure sketches
content:
Purpose
This is a working note capturing empirical runs and soft hypotheses around how bandwidth steering (active placement of tensor shards across links) interacts with backpressure buildup in our continuous-batching LLM serving pipeline. Goal: find low-effort mitigations we can ship that reduce 95p latency spikes on 8-GPU nodes under mixed-length workloads.

Context and quick recap
- Problem: under mixed short/long sequences we see occasional token-step stalls where a subset of GPUs becomes the critical path -> tail latency jumps. Hypothesis space: imbalance in NCCL rendezvous, unsmooth packetization, KV-cache hot-shard congestion, and RDMA queue saturation.
- Environment: 8xA100 (PCIE+NVLink topology), driver/kernel stack consistent with release-2025q3. Runtime: inference engine v1.9.2 with continuous-batch scheduler. Bench harness: synthetic trace w/ 60% 64-token, 40% 512-token, interarrival poisson lambda=350 qps.

Summary of experiments run (quick)
1) Per-link rate limiting (software shaping) on host NICs to create symmetric link utilization. Result: reduced variance in step times but increased median by ~5% — indicates we were smoothing bursts at cost of throughput.
2) NCCL environment tweaks (NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1, NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0) toggles: enabling IB helped cross-node but made intra-node small-mesh transfers jittery.
3) Small-packet aggregation (coalesce small msgs into 4KB chunks) in runtime transport: biggest win for short sequences (95p down 18%), negligible for long-only workloads.
4) KV-cache placement policy: moved hot prefixes to GPUDirect-local shards (replicate top-1% keys) — seemed to avoid repeated remote fetches at cost of +2% memory.

Representative log excerpt (raw timing lines from profiler, unchanged):

[step=1423] gpu0: compute 1.8ms | transfer-out 0.6ms | nccl-allreduce 4.7ms | wait 2.1ms
[step=1423] gpu1: compute 2.0ms | transfer-out 0.5ms | nccl-allreduce 9.8ms | wait 0.7ms  <-- outlier
[step=1423] gpu2: compute 1.7ms | transfer-out 0.6ms | nccl-allreduce 4.9ms | wait 1.9ms
[step=1423] gpu3: compute 1.9ms | transfer-out 0.6ms | nccl-allreduce 5.1ms | wait 1.2ms

Notes: gpu1's allreduce is double the others — suggests packetization skew or head-of-line queuing at that VC.

Micro-profiling observations
- Packet sizes: many transfers are tiny (< 512 bytes) for short sequences; NCCL tends to prefer many small send ops -> large MCQ overhead.
- NIC queues: RX queue length saturations correlate with highest allreduce times. When we artificially rate-limit other flows, the queue backlog is reduced and allreduce times normalize.
- RDMA verbs: observed occasional ENOMEM errors in kernel logs during sustained burst regimes; seems related to pinned-buffer exhaustion under many concurrent tiny ops.

Hypotheses (ranked)
1) Small-message flood creates head-of-line blocking on NIC/RDMA queues which magnifies into an NCCL slow peer -> tail latency.
2) Default block sizes in our local transport are suboptimal; aggregation/coalescing at runtime would reduce per-message overhead.
3) KV-cache remote misses amplify the frequency of short transfers during autoregressive sampling steps (many quick lookups). Replicating hot keys will reduce remote traffic bursts.
4) NCCL rendezvous scheduling can pick a suboptimal ring/fanout pattern when link load is asymmetric; forcing topology-aware algorithms may help.

Quick experiments to try next (actionable)
- Implement adaptive coalescing: if payloads < 1KB in last 500ms, buffer up to 8 messages or 4KB before send. Measure cost on median. (owner: Mateo)
- Add per-device NIC RX depth monitoring and backpressure signal to scheduler: if queue depth > threshold then slow new small requests for that device (graceful shed). (owner: Jing)
- Hot-key sampler: track top remote-accessed KV keys over a minute window and opportunistically replicate to a second device. Ensure eviction policy bounded. (owner: Ethan)
- Experiment with NCCL topo forcing flags in CI (try ring,fat-tree,tree) and run 24h mixed trace to look for shifts in 99p. (owner: Aisha)

Preliminary measurements (after quick coalescing prototype)
- Test harness: same synthetic trace. Coalescing buffer = 4KB or 8 items, flush on 500us.
- Result: 95p latency improved 16% on mixed trace, median +3%. 99p improved 8% but occasional degenerate cases still exist.

Risks/notes
- Coalescing increases per-request latency for very short lived single-message requests if we wait for buffer fill; need adaptive flushing thresholds.
- Aggressive replication (KV) increases memory pressure and may interact poorly with quantized models. Need bounded budget per model.
- Changing NCCL flags globally might affect other teams; run in isolated canary first.

Open questions and measurements to collect
- Correlate NIC queue depths (per VC) with allreduce durations across many nodes — need a 48-hour trace capture.
- Capture RDMA pinned memory usage during burst windows to validate ENOMEM root cause.
- Try selective coalescing only for traffic the profiler tags as small-message to avoid hurting long-message latency.

Decision log / next steps
- Short term (2 weeks): land opt-in runtime coalescing behind an env var; add VC queue depth metric to console (panel).
- Medium term (1–2 months): KV hot-key replication prototype; topology-aware NCCL policy tests in staging.
- Long term: work with infra to expose hardware-level queue insights (NIC telemetry) for automated steering.

Notes-to-self / random ideas
- Could we push a minimal in-band credit mechanism from NIC to runtime to signal congestion? Might be complicated but could avoid kernel-level ENOMEM spirals.
- Consider a fallback: if device's allreduce runtime > X ms for Y consecutive steps, temporarily route that shard to a replica copy for next N steps.

References and links
- github PR with proto: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1724
- jira: INF-2987 (bandwidth steering spike investigation)

Inbox TODOs
- [ ] Add telemetry: per-VC rx/tx queue depth metrics (Jing)
- [ ] Implement adaptive coalescing prototype (Mateo)
- [ ] Run 24h mixed-trace NCCL topology matrix (Aisha)
- [ ] Draft canary rollout plan for KV replication with memory guardrails (Ethan)

-- Aisha R.
(working draft, freeform notes — not yet a design doc)
